newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains as global stocks and bonds rally.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains as global stocks and bonds rally.

text.p: The dollar climbed against most major currencies Monday after remarks from senior U.S. and European finance officials reassured nervous investors and helped boost financial markets around the world.

In an interview on the "Meet the Press" television programme on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reassured world financial markets that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was merely raising a question last week about the level of the stock market, not voicing an opinion about whether prices were too high.

Greenspan sent global financial markets and the dollar tumbling on Friday when he warned the central bank must be wary when "irrational exuberance" in stock and other asset markets could hurt the economy.

On Monday at a monthly meeting of central bankers in Basle, Switzerland, German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and Bank of England Governor Eddie George jumped on the same bandwagon as Rubin saying financial markets had overreacted to Greenspan's comments.
Stock markets in the United States and Europe rebounded Monday from Friday's sharp losses, as did the U.S. bond market.
"The overnight statements from Tietmeyer, George and Rubin downplaying Greenspan's statements on Friday helped the dollar out a bit," said Brian McCarthy, market analyst at Ruesch International.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.5577 German marks and 113.50 Japanese yen, well above 1.5465 marks and 112.88 yen late on Friday.

Tietmeyer and George were not the only central bankers to affect foreign exchange trading Monday. Remarks by Swiss National Bank board member Jean-Pierre Roth pressured the Swiss franc, or "Swissy," which slid to its lowest level in 30-months against the German mark.

At the same gathering in Basle, Roth told reporters that the Swiss central bank was "pleased" with the recent weakness in the franc and was continuing a loose monetary policy that has been in effect since August.
"That would, if anything, continue to support the fact that 'Swissy' would go weaker," said David Durrant, a senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc., a consulting firm.
The Swiss economy remains in a prolonged slump. A weaker currency could help bolster economic growth by making Swiss-made exports more affordable to foreign buyers.
The dollar also gained against the Swiss currency, to 1.3285 francs from 1.3158 francs late Friday.

Currency traders Monday also looked ahead to a meeting of European Union leaders in Dublin on Friday and Saturday where officials will work toward the planned launch of a single European currency in January 1999.
Doubts that the single currency will debut as planned tend to benefit the mark by enhancing its role as Europe's premier currency.
In other trading, the British pound rose to $1.6475 late Monday from $1.6467 late on Friday. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3549 from C$1.3594.
